name: Raoult's law
seoDesc: Raoult's law: work out moles of solute (n₁) from the partial pressure of solvent and the mole fraction of solvent. A free chemistry calculator with the…
summary: The Raoult's law calculator turns the partial pressure of solvent and the mole fraction of solvent into moles of solute (n₁). It suits a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Raoult's law calculator work?
sections.html:
The Raoult's law calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports moles of solute (n₁) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select units for the chart); then you type in the partial pressure of solvent (pº) and the mole fraction of solvent (x).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in kilopascals. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 6 options, such as kPa, atm and mmHg. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Raoult's law calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Moles of solute (n₁)=-moles of solvent (n₂) × vapor pressure of solution (p) ÷ (vapor pressure of solution (p) − partial pressure of solvent (pº))
Vapor pressure of solution (p)=partial pressure of solvent (pº) × mole fraction of solvent (x)
Moles of solute (n₁)=-moles of solvent (n₂) × mole fraction of solvent (x) ÷ (mole fraction of solvent (x) − 1)
Placeholder var=(units var chart)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Partial pressure of solvent (pº) = 10 kPa, Moles of solvent (n₂) = 10 mol, Vapor pressure of solution (p) = 10 kPa and Select units for the chart set to kPa. Working through the relationship above gives Mole fraction of solvent (x) = 1.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Mole fraction of solvent (x) = 1 should be roughly the size you expected from Partial pressure of solvent (pº) = 10 kPa and Moles of solvent (n₂) = 10 mol.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals
  • Mole, opening in moles
  • Mole, opening in moles
  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Raoult's law calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the partial pressure of solvent and the mole fraction of solvent — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Raoult's law calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns moles of solute (n₁), derived from the partial pressure of solvent and the mole fraction of solvent. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Raoult's law calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the partial pressure of solvent and the mole fraction of solvent, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter partial pressure of solvent (pº) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Partial pressure of solvent (pº) opens in kilopascals and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Mole fraction of solvent (x) = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Raoult's law calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
